newsitem.title: JAPAN: DKB says its problem loans to fall to Y1.35 trln.
newsitem.headline: DKB says its problem loans to fall to Y1.35 trln.

text.p: Japan's Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank Ltd (DKB) said on Friday that its problem loans would fall to 1.35 trillion yen at the end of March from 1.83 trillion yen a year earlier.

DKB's Senior Managing Director Fumio Akanuma told a news conference that the leading commercial bank had decided to cut problem loans as much as possible in 1996/97 in order to prepare for Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms.
"To prepare for the new Big Bang financial era, we aim to strengthen the bank's financial strength by actively disposing of problem loans and to lower the costs of the corporate structure," he said.
By disposing of 550 billion yen in problem loans in 1996/97, more than half of its outstanding problem loans will be covered with loan-loss provisions, he said.

The bank's bad and non-performing loans will total 1.1 trillion yen at the end of March and non-performing loans will amount to 150 billion yen, he said. It will also have 100 billion yen in restructured loans, he added.

Bad loans are loans to bankrupt firms, non-performing loans are those on which interest payments are in arrears for six months or more and restructured loans are those on which interest payments from borrowers are cut or waived.
Earlier, the bank said it would post a parent current loss of 300 billion yen in 1996/97. This compared with the bank's previous estimate of a 40 billion yen profit for the year.

Analysts welcomed the announcement, saying it showed the bank's efforts to cut its problem loans. But they added it was not a surprise, as 17 of the top 20 banks posted losses to write off problem loans in 1995/96, when DKB posted profits.

"I cannot say that DKB will clear its bad loan mess in 1996/97," an analyst said. "Land prices are still falling and there are potential problem loans made to non-bank financial firms and construction and real estate firms."
